explanation: Paradoxical embolism through PFO causing recurrent systemic embolism D. Closure of PFO and antiplatelet therapy A PFO is present in about 25% of the population and may coexist without etiologic implications in a patient with unexplained systemic embolism.1Owing to the complexity of variables involved and the lack of rigorous scientific evidence, no position can be made regarding quantitative assessment of the role of a PFO. Therefore, this should be evaluated with critical clinical judgment in an multidisciplinary setting, weighing up the following features on an individual basis: patient characteristics, imaging stroke/infarction pattern, PFO characteristics, and case-specific clinical clues.1An atrial septal aneurysm and/or a moderate to severe shunt are strongly associated with a causal role of PFO in patients with cryptogenic stroke in observational and randomized studies.2-6 Patent foramen ovale has been associated with systemic embolism to several organs.7A cryptogenic embolic event is defined as any definite ischemia occurring in an arterial bed without a known cause despite investigation.1Patients presenting with this picture should be screened for the presence of a PFO. When a PFO is thought likely to be implicated in a presumed cryptogenic embolic event, the event should then be classified as PFO-related instead of cryptogenic.8 Randomized clinical trials have shown superiority of PFO closure in reducing risk of recurrent ischemic stroke in certain patient subsets when compared with optimal medical therapy.9For patients who are open to all options, the BMJ Rapid Recommendations panel10make a weak recommendation for PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy rather than anticoagulant therapy. In all clinical scenarios, the 2 main tenets guiding treatment of PFO are the assessments of the probability that the PFO has a relevant role in the observed clinical picture and the likelihood that the observed clinical event will recur.1For patients with the highest probability of both, closure of the PFO should be advocated. For patients with the lowest probability, medical therapy should be considered.1For patients with intermediate probabilities, clinical judgment and discussion with the patient are required in appropriate decision-making.1 The position of the European Society of Cardiology is to perform percutaneous closure of a PFO in carefully selected patients between ages 18 to 65 years with a confirmed cryptogenic stroke, transient ischemic attack, or systemic embolism and an estimated high probability of a causal role of the PFO as assessed by clinical, anatomical, and imaging features.1 In deciding on postprocedural therapy, one should consider the following factors: (1) endothelialization of the device can continue up to 5 years following implantation; (2) device thrombosis is one of the most frequent complications following implantation; and (3) premature discontinuation of therapy may be associated with minor cerebrovascular events after PFO closure.1It is reasonable to propose dual antiplatelet therapy for 1 to 6 months after PFO closure.1Therapy with a single antiplatelet agent should be continued for at least 5 years.1The extension of therapy with a single antiplatelet beyond 5 years should be based on the balance between patient’s overall risk of stroke from other causes and bleeding risk.1 As in the case of this patient, paradoxical embolism across a large PFO should be considered in cases of myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries. Patent foramen ovale closure plus 1 to 6 months of dual antiplatelet therapy postprocedure was felt to be the treatment of choice owing to an estimated high probability of a causal role of the PFO with demonstrated recurrence in systemic embolism.

caption: A, Clinical image of periorbital xanthomas. B, Diffuse lipid-laden foamy histiocytes (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the hospital with fever, joint pain, and second-degree atrioventricular block. His medical history included several years of diffuse xanthomas of the skin, peripheral hypereosinophilia, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary nodules, bilateral anterior uveitis, avascular necrosis of the wrist, and IgG κ light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. No diagnosis had been identified, and treatments had included corticosteroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated an absolute eosinophil count of 3180 cells/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; reference range, 0-400 cells/μL) and normal lipid panel results; testing results for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

caption: Dermoscopic findings of an 8-mm red nodule on the scalp show irregular red lacunae without septa and irregular linear vessels (A), and hematoxylin-eosin staining shows a vascular proliferation in dermis and subcutis composed of ectatic thin-walled vessels containing multiple branching structures (B).
scenario: An otherwise healthy man in his 40s was referred to our dermatology clinic for a slowly growing tumor on the scalp. Skin examination revealed an 8-mm red, firm, mobile nodule on the left temporal scalp. On dermoscopic evaluation, irregular red lacunae with irregular vessels and absence of septa were observed (Figure 1A and B). The lesion was excised for histopathologic analysis.
explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the lesion demonstrated a well-circumscribed dermal vascular tumor extending to the superficial subcutaneous tissue and composed of ectatic thin-walled vessels with multiple intravascular branching papillary structures (Figure 1B). These structures were covered by swollen endothelial cells with numerous intracytoplasmic eosinophilic hyaline globules, positive on periodic acid−Schiff (PAS) (Figure 2). The papillae core contained collagenous stroma, pericytes, and normal-appearing capillary vessels. Tumor vessels were positive for CD-31, and negative for D2-40 (podoplanin) and HHV-8; α-smooth muscle actin highlighted the pericytes in the papillae. The basal membrane and stroma inside the papillae were positive for collagen IV. Papillary hemangioma (PH) is a benign tumor that was first described in 2007 by Suurmeijer et al.1To our knowledge, only 16 cases have been described in the English-language literature.1-4Most of the reported cases have occurred in male adults on the head and neck.2Histopathologic mimickers of PH include tufted angioma (TA), Masson tumor (MT), intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia, and glomeruloid hemangioma (GH), among others. Most of these neoplasms exhibit intravascular capillary proliferations similar to PH. TA differs from PH in that it presents as a slow-growing plaque, most frequently in children and young adults. In some cases, this lesion has been associated with hyperhidrosis or hypertricosis. On dermoscopic examination, skin colored to light pink structureless areas have been described. TA may develop Kasabach-Merritt phenomena, which does not occur in PH. Histopathologically, TA presents multiple lobules of packed capillaries scattered throughout the dermis and the subcutis separated by normal stroma (cannonball pattern). Unlike PH, papillary structures or hyaline globules are not seen. MT is a reactive proliferation of endothelial cells secondary to an unusual thrombus within a vein, a proliferation inside a preexisting vascular lesion, or rarely, associated with a hematoma. MT affects young adults and presents as a bluish or red nodule or papule on the extremities.5Histologically, the papillary structures of MT are characterized by an acellular fibrous core coated by endothelial cells. These papillae lack capillaries, and it is sometimes possible to observe thrombosis in different stages of organization within the dilated vessel. GH is the most important PH histopathological differential diagnosis because both conditions show a proliferation of capillary vessels within a dilated vascular structure and hyaline globules; however, its clinical presentation and associated diseases differ. Clinically, GH presents as multiple, small, red papules on the trunk and limbs, with a rapid onset of days or few weeks.6,7In contrast, PH presents in adults as a solitary tumor on the head and neck. Additionally, GH is considered to be a hallmark finding of POEMS (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, skin changes)6and TAFRO (thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, and organomegaly) syndromes. PH has no associated underlying diseases. Cases reported as solitary GH without associated disease are likely PH.2,8 On dermoscopic examination, GH displays red lacunae and/or red-white backgrounds, linear irregular vessels, and red rounded structures.6,7In the present case, PH dermoscopic findings showed red lacunae without septa, white structureless areas, and irregular vessels. These findings have not been previously described. Histopathologically, there are important architectural differences among these. GH is a superficial dermal proliferation composed of a big sinusoidal central vessel with multiple capillaries inside forming loops, which resemble a kidney glomerulus. GH lacks a prominent stroma and substantial pericytes.8PH is a deep dermal to subcutaneous tumor composed of interconnected intravascular papillae with abundant stroma, pericytes, and scant capillaries. In both GH and PH, swollen endothelial cells with hyaline globules may be observed. These globules correspond to thanatosomes, secondary lysosomes that would represent cellular damage.9 In some cases, differentiating GH from PH can be challenging. Suurmeijer et al8reported that the best immunohistochemical marker to differentiate GH from PH in complex cases is collagen IV, which is abundant in the stroma and shows a thick basement membrane in PH and a thin basement membrane in GH. Recently, somatic variations inGNA11andGNAQwere described in pediatric cases of PH.GNA11andGNAQvariants could be an aid in PH differential diagnosis.10In conclusion, we report a case of PH with its clinical and histologic characteristics and describe the dermoscopic features of PH. It is important for clinicians to be familiar with this entity because confusion with GH may lead to unnecessary laboratory testing.

caption: A, Thin, deeply erythematous plaque with studded papules and pustules interspersed in the lesion located on the right anteromedial thigh. B, Photomicrograph of a hematoxylin-eosin–stained section from the right anterior thigh.
scenario: A male patient was evaluated by the dermatology inpatient consult service. He reported a 5-week history of a skin lesion on the right anterior thigh with intermittent itching and mild tenderness to palpation. There was no preceding trauma to the area. The lesion was stable in size. He denied systemic symptoms of fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath, and dyspnea on exertion. He was unhoused and sleeping on the streets with his dog prior to hospitalization. Physical examination was remarkable for a 5-cm erythematous plaque studded with papules and pustules (Figure 1A). No pus or granules could be expressed with pressure. The patient had no similar skin lesions elsewhere on the body. A 6-mm punch biopsy was obtained from the lesion. One half was sent for routine histopathology with special stains, and the other half was submitted for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial culture (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathologic sections demonstrated foci of mixed granulomatous inflammation in the deep dermis containing thick-walled fungal yeast forms with equivocal budding (Figure 2), which were highlighted by Grocott-Gömöri methenamine stain. The fungal morphology raised the possibility ofBlastomycesinfection. Further tests and evaluation, including urineBlastomycesantigen, serumBlastomycesantibodies, HIV serology, chest computed tomography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging, were unrevealing. Given the unremarkable imaging, the patient was diagnosed with a deep dermal fungal infection, possibly representing primary cutaneous blastomycosis. While fungal culture results were pending, he began taking empirical itraconazole, 200 mg, 3 times daily for 3 days, followed by itraconazole, 200 mg, 2 times daily for an additional 1 to 2 weeks with input from the infectious disease department. Despite attempts to reach the patient, he was lost to follow-up after hospital dismissal. The fungal cultures ultimately grewTrichophyton verrucosum3 weeks later. The treatment plan outlined herein was considered adequate, if followed as directed. Dermatophyte infections occur frequently worldwide and often affect the stratum corneum, hair, and nails. Most infections in humans are caused by 3 types of dermatophytes:Trichophyton, Microsporum, andEpidermophyton.1In immunocompetent hosts, these dermatophytes may not penetrate beyond the stratum granulosum. Severe dermatophytosis is not well described but can be generally categorized as extensive or invasive. Invasive dermatophytosis is defined by dermal invasion that presents in 2 clinical forms: Majocchi granuloma or deep dermatophytosis.2 Primary cutaneous blastomycosis should be included in the differential diagnosis because it demonstrates round thick-walled yeast forms with broad-based budding.3In this patient’s scenario, urine antigen and serum antibodies forBlastomyceswere negative; additionally, cultures grewTrichophyton. Given the infrequency of deep dermatophytosis in an immunocompetent host, as well as the fact that the patient lived in an area endemic forBlastomyces, blastomycosis was originally favored as a result of availability bias. It was important to avoid premature closure, particularly given the negative serum and urine test results forBlastomyces. Three prior case reports have illustratedT rubruminfection mimickingBlastomyces, with sporelike shapes and pseudobudding on histological findings.3-5This ambiguity in fungal morphology reaffirms the importance of verifying organism classification through polymerase chain reaction or fungal culture to ensure appropriate therapy and systemic evaluation. Granulomatous pyoderma gangrenosum could be considered in the differential diagnosis because it also showcases granulomatous and suppurative inflammation on histopathology.6However, there is usually ulceration with undermined edges. Fungi would not be identified on special stains. Furthermore, pyoderma gangrenosum is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other causes of mixed dermal inflammation must be ruled out.6Cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome is a rare histopathologic variant of Sweet syndrome named for the presence of basaloid, pseudoyeast forms on tissue that do not actually represent fungus.7,8These forms are negative with fungal special stains, vacuolated in a way that mimics encapsulation, and smaller than those seen here. Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma typically presents with a monomorphic infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes, which show a predilection for the epidermis and may form Pautrier microabscesses.6Oftentimes, lymphocytes show irregular nuclear contours and may display cerebriform or convoluted nuclei,6which were not seen in the histopathology of the present patient. Although there is no standardized treatment for deep dermatophytosis, systemic antifungals such as terbinafine, fluconazole, and itraconazole have been reported to be efficacious.4,9Clinicians should remain suspicious of fungi as a potential cause of deep-tissue infection in both immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients. Fungal culture or polymerase chain reaction should be performed to confirm pathogen speciation.

caption: A, Erythematous annular thin plaques without surface change on the patient’s right cheek and an erythematous, edematous plaque on the patient’s nose. B, Erythematous, edematous, annular papules and plaques on the patient’s left upper arm.
scenario: An 11-year-old girl presented to the dermatology clinic in autumn with an asymptomatic rash on her arms, face, and legs of a 3-week duration. She was otherwise healthy with a history of having seasonal allergies and taking cetirizine. She had negative results from the review of systems and denied any recent illnesses, vaccinations, or new medications. Physical examination was notable for erythematous annular thin plaques without surface change on her right cheek (Figure 1A), an erythematous, edematous plaque on her nose (Figure 1A), and erythematous, edematous, annular papules and plaques on her arms, hands, and thighs (Figure 1B). A biopsy specimen was obtained from the right arm for histopathologic analysis.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed a subtle thickened basement membrane zone and lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate (Figure 2). The patient was prescribed topical corticosteroids. Two months later, the patient presented to the dermatology clinic for worsening rash and new sun sensitivity. Laboratory examination revealed positive findings for speckled antinuclear antibodies (titers ≥1:160), antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies, antiribonucleoprotein antibodies, and anti-Ro/Sjögren syndrome A antibodies. Complete blood count test results showed leukopenia (white blood cell count of 0.003/μL). Aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels were elevated at 59 U/L and 69 U/L, respectively. The patient’s mother at this time reported that the patient had been fatigued more recently with nonspecific abdominal and shoulder pain. The patient demonstrated overlapping features of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) and subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE), pointing to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She had antinuclear antibody levels of more than 1:80 (entry-level criterion) and had 21 weighted points across 4 different domains according to the American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria for the diagnosis of SLE (the minimum requirement is 10 points). Therefore, her disease was classified as SLE.1 The patient’s rash improved dramatically with sun protection. Referred to the rheumatology division, she started a 200-mg hydroxychloroquine regimen 5 days per week (<5 mg/kg/d). The results of a liver evaluation pointed to lupus hepatitis. Test results for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, celiac disease, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and elevated α1-fetoprotein were negative. This case report details a unique presentation of ACLE and SCLE overlapping as initial signs of SLE in a pediatric patient. Cutaneous lupus erythematosus can be subdivided into the acute, subacute, and chronic forms. In pediatric patients, the chronic form is most common, while the acute and subacute forms are rare. Because the subacute form (SCLE) is exceedingly rare in the pediatric population, this presentation is even more distinctive. The localized form of ACLE may present as photosensitivity and the characteristic butterfly malar rash, sparing the nasolabial folds, while generalized ACLE can present as a morbilliform rash on sun-exposed skin. SCLE classically presents in patients as annular psoriasiform erythematous plaques without scarring.2,3This patient exhibited photosensitivity consistent with ACLE and annular plaques on her arms that were consistent with SCLE. The plaques on her arms lacked scales; although common in SCLE, scales are not necessary for diagnosis. This overlapping presentation of ACLE and SCLE in a pediatric patient has not yet been described in the literature, to our knowledge, and thus may be underrecognized. Differential diagnosis of an erythematous annular eruption with no surface change in a pediatric patient includes urticaria, polymorphous light eruption (PMLE), and interstitial granulomatous drug reaction (IGD). Urticaria is defined as the sudden development of pruritic transient wheals and angioedema or both. The histopathologic characteristics include upper dermal edema with a mild mixed perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and neutrophils. The interface dermatitis that was noted in this case is not a typical feature of urticaria. Additionally, the rash found in this patient was completely asymptomatic and was not transient.4 PMLE, a common photodermatosis, causes pruritic lesions on sun-exposed skin, sparing the face. The photosensitive cutaneous manifestations of lupus erythematosus can be difficult to distinguish from PMLE. The presence of antinuclear antibodies was an early differentiating criterion, but recent studies have established that patients with PMLE can also have elevated antinuclear antibody titers. The histologic characteristics of PMLE are nonspecific and may not distinguish PMLE from lupus erythematosus. In this case, the onset of symptoms in autumn, in addition to joint pain, leukopenia, and facial rash, makes PMLE less likely.5 IGD can have a wide clinical presentation. The skin lesions are usually asymptomatic and have a predilection for the trunk and extremities. The histologic characteristics of IGD are characterized by histiocytes scattered throughout the dermis typically arranged around foci of degenerated collagen and may form small granulomas. The histopathologic characteristics in this case did not include histiocytes but instead, an interface dermatitis that would not be seen in IGD.6 Diagnosing annular erythematous eruptions in pediatric patients can be challenging. This case report highlights diverse lupus erythematosus presentations, emphasizing the need for a thorough workup for prompt diagnosis and treatment.

caption: On examination, there were scattered, well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques with an atrophic center with a slightly elevated edge on the scrotum, buttock, groin, and intergluteal cleft (A). Biopsy findings included hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic column (cornoid lamella), and several dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the epidermal invagination with hypogranulosis and perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis (B; hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A man in his 40s presented with a 10-year history of pruritic lesions on the scrotum and buttock. He was diagnosed with eczema and treated at the local clinic with little improvement. He had no relevant medical history and no family history of similar skin problems. Physical examination revealed scattered, well-defined, annular gray hyperkeratotic plaques with an atrophic center and a slightly elevated edge on the scrotum, buttock, groin, and intergluteal cleft (Figure 1A). There was no inguinal adenopathy, and results of routine blood work, including blood biochemistry, syphilis serologies, and HIV testing, were normal or negative. We took 2 specimens from the scrotum and buttock, respectively, for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathological examination of both specimens revealed hyperkeratosis, irregular papillomatosis, parakeratotic columns (cornoid lamella) overlying dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and hypogranulosis with a perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis (Figure 2). Based on the skin lesion location and clinical and histological findings, a diagnosis of genital porokeratosis (GP) was confirmed. The patient was treated with topical imiquimod cream with good response, and the plaques became thinner with focal disappearance. He is receiving regular medication and follow-up. Porokeratosis is a group of epidermal keratotic disorders characterized by well-demarcated annular lesions with cornoid lamella histologically. Porokeratosis can affect the whole body surface but rarely involves the genitogluteal area. GP, a rare variant of porokeratosis, presents as pruritic or asymptomatic centrally atrophic annular plaques with raised keratotic margins involving the penis, scrotum, or vulva. Biopsy findings include 1 or a few cornoid lamella on histopathology.1 GP mostly affects middle-aged to elderly men and has no family history.1The cause remains unclear. Repeated frictional and scratching trauma due to the humid climate, tight-fitting underclothes, or a contact reaction to some agents may contribute to the pathogenesis of GP.2Some factors, such as genetic variation, environmental change, immunosuppression, drug intake, virus infection, and UV exposure, also may play an important role. Once diagnosis is clarified, porokeratosis should be actively treated because of its potential malignant transformation. In general, the risk of cancer is greater in long-standing, larger lesions; among elderly and immunocompromised patients; and in the clinical types of linear porokeratosis and porokeratosis of Mibelli. GP is relatively difficult to diagnose due to its rarity. The diagnosis of GP is based on the clinical and histopathological manifestations. Dermoscopic findings can assist in the diagnosis with demarcated annular lesions and central pigmentation with dotted vessels surrounded by a keratotic peripheral rim.3,4 Clinically, GP may mimic verruca vulgaris,5but the latter is typically not annular and presents as papillomatous papules and plaques, and pathological findings include hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and identifiable koilocytes, associated with fingerlike vascular-pattern features surrounded by whitish halos in dermoscopy. Bowenoid papulosis presents as isolated or multiple red-brown papules and plaques in the anogenital area with a skin biopsy demonstrating acanthosis with full-thickness epidermal atypia, and dermoscopic findings include brown linear dots or globules as well as glomerular vascular structures.6Porokeratosis ptychotropica appears as verrucous plaques in a butterfly pattern, mostly involving the natal cleft and the buttocks but sometimes also on the genital area. Often, biopsy findings include multiple cornoid lamellae.7 Therapeutically, surgical treatment includes excision, cryosurgery, dermabrasion, electrodesiccation, and carbon dioxide laser vaporization.8,9For more widespread lesions, long-term medication management, including topical 5-fluorouracil, 5%; topical calcipotriol; imiquimod cream; and oral aromatic retinoids, may treat the disease.2However, it has been difficult to develop therapeutic protocols for GP due to underreporting. Most patients have only symptomatic relief with poor response to various treatments.

caption: A, Multiple pink papules and umbilicated nodules on the face. B, Numerous yeasts surrounded by hyaline capsules (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A man in his 20s presented to the dermatology department with a monthlong history of gradually progressing papules and nodules on the face, accompanied by fever, fatigue, and weight loss. On physical examination, multiple pink papules and umbilicated nodules were found on the face (Figure 1A). He had a 5-year history of HIV infection but self-discontinued his antiretroviral treatment due to treatment-related gastrointestinal and neurologic reactions 4 years prior. A biopsy specimen was taken for pathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathology of a biopsy specimen showed numerous yeast forms surrounded by clear spaces (Figure 1B andFigure 2). The white blood cell count was 2040/μL, and the CD4-positive lymphocyte count was 2/μL (to convert both to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were found in the neck, axilla, groin, and posterior peritoneum. Capsular polysaccharide antigen ofCryptococcus neoformansin the serum and cerebrospinal fluid was positive. Fungal cultures of blood and cerebrospinal fluid were also identified asC neoformans. T-cell spot test for tuberculous was negative. A diagnosis of disseminated cryptococcosis was made. Liposomal amphotericin B and fluconazole were given to treat cryptococcosis, and antiretroviral therapy was restarted for HIV infection. The cutaneous symptoms resolved after 2 months. Fungi are major contributors to the opportunistic infections and death in patients with HIV/AIDS.1,2Cryptococcosis can affect any organ system, especially the brain, lungs, skin, bones, and vasculature, and is often generalized.3Cutaneous manifestations of cryptococcosis include acneiform papules, molluscum contagiosum–like lesions, Kaposi sarcoma–like lesions, ulcers, pustules, plaques such as eczematous plaques, nodules, abscesses, subcutaneous swellings, and cellulitis.1There are 2 histopathologic types: granulomatous and gelatinous. The former type shows fewer yeasts and scant necrosis, while the latter type is characterized by numerous organisms with little inflammation. The yeast is oval, measuring 5 to 12 μm in diameter, enclosed by a capsule that presents as an empty space around yeast in hematoxylin-eosin preparations.4These yeasts are not actually intracellular. Umbilicated rash is a typical skin feature of cryptococcosis in immunocompromised patients and needs to be distinguished from talaromycosis5and histoplasmosis.6A comprehensive evaluation is necessary to make diagnostic confirmation by laboratory testing and biopsies of affected areas. Talaromycosis is an opportunistic mycosis caused byTalaromyces marneffei(formerlyPenicillium marneffei), which is a dimorphic fungus. A biopsy specimen exhibits numerous round fungal structures, 2 to 4 μm in diameter, packed within histiocytes or scattered through the tissue. Tissue culture growsT marneffei.7Histoplasmosis, a widespread disease, is caused by 2 distinct organisms in humans:Histoplasma capsulatumvarduboisiiandHistoplasma capsulatumvarcapsulatum. Common skin lesions of histoplasmosis include hemorrhagic, maculopapular eruption, and ulceration; patients with HIV are at higher risk for infection. Histopathologic examination of histoplasmosis lesions reveals dermal granuloma with small, narrow-budding yeasts often found within macrophages. Anti-Histoplasmaantibodies can be detected.8Lobomycosis is a chronic, deep fungal infection caused byLacazia loboi.It is characterized by the appearance of slowly developing keloidlike cutaneous lesions. Histopathological assessment shows dermal granulomas with multinucleated giant cells filled with fungal cells 6 to 12 μm in diameter with doubly refractile walls.9 Diagnosis requires a high level of clinical awareness and confirmation by culture and histopathology. Criterion-standard antifungal therapy remains the combination of amphotericin B deoxycholate and flucytosine.2

caption: Soft green-blue plaque on the dorsal hand.
scenario: An otherwise healthy woman in her 30s presented with a painful bruise on her hand that initially appeared a few days after she sustained a twisting injury to the affected hand while participating in acroyoga 2 years before. Since the initial onset, the bruise and pain had persisted despite icing and resting the area. She denied any personal or family history of bleeding disorders. On examination, an ill-defined indurated blue-green plaque was noted on the dorsum of the left hand (Figure 1). Radiography results showed soft tissue swelling but were otherwise unremarkable. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneously fluid hyperintense and T1 heterogeneously hyperintense lesion measuring approximately 1.6 × 0.5 × 2.9 cm that was centered within the dorsal subcutaneous soft tissue of the hand. An excision was performed.
explanation: Diagnosis of hemosiderotic fibrolipomatous tumor (HFLT) was confirmed, with pathology results demonstrating mixed fibrous and mature adipose tissue with extensive pigment deposition (Figure 2A). Lesional cells were spindled, ovoid, and epithelioid, with open chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and without mitoses (Figure 2B). A mixed inflammatory infiltrate that included neutrophils, histiocytes, and foamy macrophages was present. Immunohistochemistry results were strongly positive for CD34 (Figure 2C) in the lesional cells but negative for S100, SRY-box transcription factor 10 (SOX10), human melanoma black 45 (HMB45), and Melan-A (not shown). The HFLT tumor is a rare, slow-growing painful subcutaneous mass characterized by varying proportions of mature adipocytes, spindle cells, and hemosiderin pigment.1These tumors typically stain positive for CD34 and negative for desmin, smooth muscle actin, keratin, and S100.2While HFLTs predominantly occur on the foot and ankle, these tumors can also occur elsewhere on the body, including the hand and/or wrist in up to 10% of reported cases.1-7 First described in 2000, the HFLT was initially thought to represent a reactive inflammatory process because 7 of these 8 reported cases had a history of trauma that occurred in the same area where the HFLT later occurred.1Kazakov et al8proposed that vascular insufficiency contributes to HFLT pathogenesis, although the discovery of a chromosomal translocation t(1;10)(p22;q24) and/orTGFBR3/MGEA5rearrangement(s) in 17 cases has suggested a potential primary neoplastic origin of this diagnosis.5,7,9The exact prevalence of prior trauma in HFLT cases has been difficult to enumerate due to varying definitions and inconsistent histories. Of the 31 patients reviewed by Moretti et al,313 of 28 (46%) were found to have a history of trauma or vasculopathy. Currently, some believe that HFLT could be neoplastic and reactive, and that trauma and/or blood vessel damage could contribute to the morphogenesis10; however, further research is needed. To our knowledge, only 1 prior HFLT of the hand has been associated with prior trauma. This involved a patient who smashed his hand on a pipe before development of the tumor.1To our knowledge, twisting or sports-related injuries, such as in the current patient’s case, have not been reported in the development of HFLT involving the upper extremity, wrist, or hand, and this highlights the emerging dangers of activities such as acroyoga. The HFLT can have a similar histological appearance to other tumors, which stresses the importance of clinical history and high clinical suspicion. Pigmented epithelioid melanocytoma is a distinct melanoma subtype that can occur in younger patients and is heavily pigmented and characterized by spindled cells on pathology. Immunohistochemistry results would stain positive for melanocyte markers, such as S100, SOX10, and HMB45 and would be negative for CD34. Pigmented dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSPs) exhibit CD34-positive spindle cells but would stain positive for Melan-A, which was negative in this case. Furthermore, pigmented DFSPs may demonstrate isolated positivity for S100 in pigment-laden dendritic cells. Lesional cells of DFSP are often arranged in a whirling and storiform architecture, without substantial cytologic atypia. Given the presence of foamy macrophages in this case, along with tumor cell morphology and immunohistochemical and architectural findings, pigmented DFSP was excluded. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytomas typically show a multinodular lesion with a fibrous pseudocapsule consisting of granulomatous-appearing epithelioid to spindle cells that are accompanied by hemosiderin deposits. However, peripheral lymphoid aggregates are a characteristic feature. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma also shows epithelial membrane antigen positivity andEWSR1gene rearrangement. In conclusion, HFLT is a rare and only recently described entity. The exact pathogenesis of HFLT has not yet been clarified, and the role trauma plays in its development needs further investigation. Regardless, a reliable history of prior trauma has been reported, and clinicians should be on high alert of similar appearing lesions that appear after various injuries, including those involving physical activity and sports. Additionally, clinicians should counsel patients on HFLT’s relatively high recurrence rate (30% to 50%) and that malignant transformation and distant metastases are very rare.10

caption: Clinical images of keratotic papules diffusely distributed on an extremity, original (A) and magnified (B).
scenario: A woman in her 50s presented with a 3-month history of rapidly spreading intensively pruritic papules on her extremities. The lesions consisted of scattered, erythematous, annular papules measuring up to 5 mm wide (Figure 1). Further examination revealed a few asymptomatic brown flat papules scattered on her face; the palms, soles, and oral mucosa were not involved. The patient had no remarkable medical or family history and was not concurrently being treated with any medications. She had been previously diagnosed with eczema and treated with topical steroid ointments and oral compound glycyrrhizin tablets, which had no obvious effect. Laboratory investigations, including routine blood, liver and kidney function, antistreptolysin O, C-reactive protein, antinuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor tests, disclosed no abnormal findings. A biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic examination.
explanation: C. Eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis (EPPP) The skin biopsy specimen from an annular lesion revealed mild hyperkeratosis accompanied by parakeratosis, atrophy of the epidermis, well-developed cornoid lamellae with a decreased granular layer, individual cell dyskeratosis, and vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer (Figure 2A). There was a slight infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils in the upper dermis (Figure 2B). A diagnosis of EPPP was established. Six months after the patient’s first visit, the papules began to subside spontaneously without any medication, leaving sporadic brown annular keratotic lesions. Eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis is a rare variant of porokeratosis, presenting with acute exacerbation of annular papules surrounded by a distinctive hyperkeratotic ridgelike border accompanied by severe pruritus; it has also been called eruptive disseminated porokeratosis (EDP).1-3Shoimer and colleagues categorized EDP into 4 subtypes: paraneoplastic, immunosuppressed, inflammatory, and other type.1In the present case, the asymptomatic brown papules on the patient’s face were consistent with disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis; however, the lesions distributed over the non−sun-exposed flexor surfaces of the extremities differed from this condition. According to Shoimer and colleagues’ proposed classification, the lesions on the extremities should be considered to be an EDP of the inflammatory subtype. Histologically, the presence of a cornoid lamella and a dermal inflammatory infiltrate are the most frequent findings.2Approximately 25% to 50% of patients with EPPP show additional eosinophilic infiltration in the vicinity of blood vessels in the upper dermis.3 Differential diagnoses of EPPP include annular lichen planus (ALP), perforating granuloma annulare (PGA), and atypical pityriasis rosea (APR). A rare clinical variant of lichen planus, ALP presents with a slightly raised annular edge and central clearing.4The annular edge is typically purple to white and the central portion is hyperpigmented or skin colored.4Individual lesions range in size from 0.5 to 2.5 cm.4Generalized eruptions of ALP are rarely described.4Few patients have pruritus.4Sites of involvement include the axilla, penis, extremities, groin, and other areas.4Histologically, ALP is associated with hyperkeratosis without parakeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, and a bandlike lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction, whereas EPPP is associated with cornoid lamella with a decreased granular layer.5 Another differential diagnosis is PGA, which may present as an umbilicated papule with a central crust or hyperkeratotic core on the extremities or trunk with lesions that become pustular or ulcerate; it is a condition more commonly reported in children.6Eruptions are usually asymptomatic, although pruritus and pain have been reported.7Histologically, PGA is characterized by mucinous collagen degeneration surrounded by palisading granulomas with transepithelial elimination of altered collagen.6 In diagnosing EPPP, it is also important to exclude APR, which commonly presents as papular, vesicular, and purpuric lesions.8Most of the lesions follow a course similar to the classic form of pityriasis rosea.9A herald patch is an important marker, which is seen in most of the atypical cases, and atypia is rare in herald patches.8The involvement of the face, scalp, hands, and feet is unusual, and pityriasis rosea of the fingers, scalp, eyelids, and penis is exceptional.9Itching may be severe, with pain and burning sensation in some cases.9Histopathologic examination reveals focal parakeratosis in the epidermis, spongiosis, extravasation of red blood cells, and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.8 There is no standard treatment for EPPP. Topical corticosteroids and antihistamines are the most frequently used treatment, but response is often poor.2Topical fluorouracil, etretinate, assisted freezing, and laser therapy have been used, but their effectiveness is unsatisfactory.2A topical vitamin D3analogue, maxacalcitol, may be effective against pruritic papules.3 Because EPPP may be associated with various neoplasms (31% of cases) and viral infections (2% of cases), screening for malignant neoplasms is recommended. For 75% of EPPP cases, resolution is spontaneous after 6 months2; therefore, screening for tumors is important, if clinically indicated.2

caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody–positive systemic sclerosis complicated by scleroderma kidney crisis, heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon while receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily, presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).
explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

caption: A, Erythematous plaques involving the right chest and flank at the initial presentation. B and C, Large atypical cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm forming papillary and glandular architectures are present in the deep dermis; lymphovascular invasion was observed in the superficial and deep dermis (hematoxylin-eosin). D, Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis showing a large heterogeneous mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle (blue arrowhead) and cystic lesion in the left ovary (pink arrowhead).
scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with painful erythematous plaques on her trunk (Figure, A). Skin lesions developed 2 months earlier and progressively spread. She reported abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and vaginal bleeding. A solid mass on her lower abdomen that had been palpable about 10 years prior had rapidly increased in size within the past few months. Physical examination revealed erythematous plaques on the right chest and flank without warmth. Punch biopsy of a lesion from the chest was sent for histopathological examination (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Results of histopathological examination showed atypical cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles forming a glandular architecture in the deep dermis, and lymphovascular invasion was observed (Figure, B and C). Immunohistochemical staining results were positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, estrogen receptors (ERs), GATA-binding protein 3, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, Wilms tumor 1 (WT1), and thyroid transcription factor-1. Findings from chest and abdominopelvic computed tomography revealed a 13-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle and a 3-cm ovarian cystic lesion (Figure, D). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography findings revealed intense abnormal18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the abdominal wall, lung, liver, and lymph nodes. Laboratory examinations revealed increased concentrations of lactate dehydrogenase (558 U/L; reference, 135-214 U/L; to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), cancer antigen 15-3 (143.8 U/mL; reference, <26.4 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and cancer antigen 125 (2528 U/mL; reference, <35 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level (2.2 ng/mL; reference, <6 ng/mL; to convert to μg/L, multiply by 1.0). The patient underwent debulking surgery, and pathologic examination revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma positive for MOC31, napsin A, and PAX8, and negative for calretinin, WT1, CK5/6, ERs, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and p53. The patient was diagnosed with primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma (PPCCC) with multiple distant metastases. She underwent chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin, but the disease progressed continuously. Another metastatic lesion developed in her abdomen. Despite treatment with topotecan and cisplatin, she died 6 months after the initial diagnosis. Primary peritoneal carcinoma (PPC) is a rare malignant epithelial tumor, and PPCCC is an extremely rare subtype of PPC, with only 15 cases, to our knowledge, having been reported since 1990.1Because of its rarity, the clinical characteristics of PPCCC are not well understood. In the previous reports, all patients with PPCCC were female, and the average age was 53.7 years. The initial symptoms included abdominal pain, distension, and an abdominopelvic solid mass. Imaging studies commonly revealed large heterogeneous cystic and solid masses with a mean size of 13 cm. Histologically, PPCCC closely resembles primary peritoneal serous carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. For diagnosis, extensive immunohistochemical staining is required. Primary peritoneal serous carcinoma expresses CK7, ERs, and WT1, but PPCCC is typically negative for WT1.1Malignant mesothelioma is typically positive for CK5/6, calretinin, and WT1, and negative for MOC31, but PPCCC shows the opposite features.1 Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis usually manifests as indurated erythematous to violaceous plaques symmetrically distributed on the lateral trunk and proximal extremities.2Histologically, interstitial and perivascular histiocytic infiltrates with small foci of collagen degeneration are observed in the reticular dermis.3Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is often associated with rheumatic diseases, hematologic disorders, and internal cancers, but pathogenesis of interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is currently not well understood.3Wolf isotopic response is a rare cutaneous reaction in which a new and unrelated dermatosis occurs at the site of a previously healed dermatosis, most commonly in areas of post–varicella-zoster virus scarring.4Histologically, granulomatous and lichenoid reactions were frequently reported.5Cutaneous endometriosis usually manifests as reddish-brown nodules on the umbilicus or a firm mass on the scar site. Histopathological examination shows the columnar epithelium surrounded by stroma, which consists of capillary vessels, fibroblasts, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.6 To our knowledge, cutaneous metastasis of PPCCC has not yet been reported. Primary peritoneal carcinoma most commonly metastasizes within the peritoneal cavity; metastases to the skin, liver, brain, lung, and breast are rarely reported.7Because PPC behaves similarly to ovarian carcinoma,7,8PPC may also manifest with lesions similar to those associated with ovarian carcinomas, such as inflammatory metastases, cicatricial plaques, or cellulitislike or lymphangitislike lesions,9and similar features can be expected in PPCCC. Patients with PPCCC are commonly treated with debulking surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma is considered to have a poor prognosis because the majority of patients die of the disease within 6 months or experience recurrence within 3 years.10Because of the poor prognosis, prompt diagnosis and optimal treatment are required.

scenario: A man in his 40s with a medical history of factor VII deficiency hemophilia presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure secondary to COVID-19. Following admission, he was intubated with prone positioning, and treatment with tocilizumab and dexamethasone was started. He was also found to haveStaphylococcus hemolyticusbacteremia, and treatment with cefepime was initiated. Three days after admission, the patient developed erythema and edematous necrotic plaques of the bilateral ears (Figure, A and B). No devices had been used on the ears. The necrosis progressed during the following days, primarily involving the earlobe of the right ear and a large portion of the helix of the left ear. A punch biopsy specimen was performed (Figure, C and D).
explanation: Results of the biopsy specimen of the left ear revealed epidermal and dermal necrosis and ulceration; there was also necrosis of the eccrine glands (Figure, D). Although eccrine necrosis is not a specific finding, it is a consistent finding in pressure necrosis. The necrotic plaques improved and then resolved after prone positioning was discontinued and further pressure on the ears was avoided. Pressure necrosis occurs from a lack of blood flow secondary to mechanical stress on the skin. Pressure necrosis in patients who are bedridden involves the sacral region. However, patients who are persistently hypoxemic often require prone positioning, subjecting other anatomic sites to prolonged pressures that exceed local capillary pressure.1Prone positioning, often greater than 16 hours a day, is used as a therapy for moderate-to-severe cases of COVID-19 that require intubation. A retrospective cohort study highlighted the high incidence of facial pressure injuries in patients with severe COVID-19 who require prone positioning (47.6%), with a substantial association of duration of proning with ulcer development.2 The differential diagnoses included levamisole-induced vasculitis. Levamisole, a synthetic imidazothiazole anthelminthic agent, is used as a cocaine-bulking agent and can produce painful purpuric macules and papules on the face and helix of the ears that progress to skin necrosis. Neutropenia is a common finding, but the diagnosis of levamisole-induced vasculitis depends heavily on a drug history. Additionally, histopathologic findings would have demonstrated a thrombotic vasculopathy with prominent fibrin thrombi.3 The incidence of acroischemia was shown to be 23% among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome associated with COVID-194and is secondary to complement-mediated microvascular injury and the hypercoagulable state of COVID-19. A diagnosis of  acroischemia is less likely, however, because the patient had no laboratory coagulation abnormalities, and histopathologic results did not show findings of thrombotic vasculopathy. Additionally, acroischemia typically involves additional acral sites beyond the ears.5 Ecthyma gangrenosum (EG) presents with gangrenous ulcers with an erythematous and edematous base and affects critically ill patients.Pseudomonas aeruginosaaccounts for 74% of cases of EG, but other gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria can cause EG.6Histopathologic findings would have demonstrated a vasculitis or vasculopathy, often with direct invasion of vessels by the causative organism. Because of the global COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a dramatic increase in the number of patients requiring prone positioning. Although it may be possible to alleviate and minimize this complication by frequent repositioning and protective padding, clinicians should be aware of the potential for this complication in patients with COVID-19 who require extended periods of ventilation support.

B, Histopathologic image showing dilated and thrombosed lymphatic vessels in subcutaneous tissue with recanalization (hematoxylin-eosin). C, Histopathologic image of partially thrombosed vessels. D, Immunohistochemistry finding was positive for D2-40 (podoplanin).
scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of multiple sclerosis consulted for the sudden development of 2 adjacent nodules on the left arm. An excision with 1-cm margins of the left arm demonstrated desmoplastic melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1 mm, and a left axillary sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) had been performed 3 weeks before under general anesthesia. The patient was also being treated with subcutaneous interferon beta 1a for the multiple sclerosis. Physical examination revealed 2 indurated and mobile subcutaneous nodules on the anterior surface of the arm 5 cm distal to the surgical scar, the larger of them measuring 15 mm in diameter (Figure, A) and the smaller of them measuring 4 mm. When the arm was abducted to 90°, the patient denied pain but described a subtle tightness sensation on the arm. An excisional biopsy from the larger lesion was performed (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Associated with the clinical findings, a subtle cord that projected from the largest nodule to the axillary region could be seen in physical examination (Figure, A). An excisional biopsy of the larger lesion showed the presence of dilated and thrombosed vessels in the subcutaneous tissue, with signs of recanalization. Other features present were edema, areas of acute hemorrhage, recent fibrosis, and focal steatonecrosis, without evidence of malignant melanoma (Figure, B). An immunohistochemical study confirmed the lymphatic vascular origin of the lesion, with expression for CD31, ERG and D2-40 (podoplanin) antibodies. Human herpesvirus 8 test results were  negative. In this setting, a Sox10 staining was also performed, ruling out a metastasis of melanoma. The medical history of a left axillary SLNB associated with the clinical, pathological, and special staining findings confirmed the diagnosis of axillary web syndrome (AWS). Axillary web syndrome is a frequently described complication in breast cancer SLNB surgical procedures, and a few cases have also been reported after SLNB for cutaneous malignant melanoma. Axillary web syndrome commonly appears within the 12 weeks after the surgical procedure.1,2It is clinically characterized by palpable tight cords in the axilla that can extend to the arm, antecubital space, and forearm, associated with pain and movement restriction of the affected segment.2Rarely, AWS can present as painless, mobile subcutaneous nodules in the ipsilateral arm of the SLNB, as observed in this patient.3The possible mechanism of the cord formation is the disruption of superficial lymphatics and vessels of the arm during SLNB surgery that cause thrombosis.3,4The histopathology of AWS is characterized by dilated and thrombosed superficial veins, lymphatics, or both.2,3The characteristic positivity of D2-40 stain in AWS strongly suggests its lymphatic origin.5A wide spectrum of differential diagnoses must be considered for sudden nodules appearing in a  postoperative patient with melanoma. Masson tumor (intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia) is a rare vascular tumor characterized by intravascular proliferation of endothelial cells that presents more frequently in female patients as a painless, slow-growing tumor in head and neck and rarely in upper extremities. It is characterized by intravascular proliferation of endothelial cells with papillary formations, almost always associated with some thrombus. Each papillary frond is covered by plump endothelial cells.6These tumors are commonly D2-40 negative and CD31, CD34, alpha smooth muscle actin, and factor VIII–related antigen positive in cells lining the papillae of Masson tumor.6,7 Melanoma is an aggressive tumor with a high ability to metastasize. Melanoma metastases typically show proliferation of atypical melanocytes and, in challenging cases, immunohistochemical markers such as Sox-10, HMB-45, Melan A, andMITFwill reveal a melanocytic differentiation.8 Pseudo-aneurysms of the brachial artery are infrequent lesions caused by trauma or iatrogenic damage after surgical interventions. They appear as growing, painful, pulsatile masses associated with tenderness and swelling under the traumatic/scar area. The walls of the pseudo-aneurysm contain variable amounts of laminated clot, surrounded by dense fibrous tissue reaction, marked accumulation of endothelial and muscle cells and deposition of proteoglycans.9The D2-40 immunohistochemical marker result is also negative. The diagnosis of AWS must be considered in patients who have undergone a recent SLNB procedure for cutaneous melanoma and develop sudden subcutaneous nodules near surgical scars. The detection of a palpable cord, frequently subtle, adjacent to the nodule, may help confirm the diagnosis of AWS rather than other less favorable diagnoses, such as melanoma metastases.

caption: A, Pustular eruption of the face characterized by monomorphous 1- to 2-mm pustules over background erythema on the cheeks, chin, and nose appearing less than 24 hours after sun exposure. Punch biopsy of skin demonstrated intrafollicular (B and C) and subcorneal (B and D) pustule formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A woman in her 20s was referred for evaluation of a 4-year history of recurrent pustular eruptions on her face, which initially presented while she was vacationing in Florida. She noted mild associated pruritus but denied burning sensation. The eruptions occurred intermittently, appearing as erythematous papules with prominent pustules, and were exacerbated by sunlight. On average, her lesions would resolve in 3 to 4 days with only mild background erythema by 5 to 7 days. Even mild sun exposure would induce the eruption, leading to frequent recurrences in summer months but long periods of remission in the fall through spring. Trials with various broad-spectrum sunscreens in combination with topical and oral antibiotics and topical ivermectin did not prevent flares or mitigate severity of eruptions when they occurred. She denied joint pain, fever, fatigue, changes in urine color, use of other topical or systemic medications, or presence of rashes elsewhere. She was otherwise healthy without other medical history. On physical examination, she was well appearing with numerous 1- to 2-mm monomorphous pustules over background erythema on the medial cheeks, chin, and nose (Figure, A). No nail fold capillary changes or mucosal lesions were observed. Serum analysis results for antinuclear, anti-SSA/Ro, and anti-SSB/La antibodies were negative. A 4-mm punch biopsy was taken from a representative lesion along the right jawline (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed subcorneal and follicular pustules (Figure, B-D). Periodic acid–Schiff and Grocott methenamine silver stain results were negative for fungal organisms. Bacterial swab results from malar lesions were negative for growth. Considering failure of multiple treatments effective for papulopustular rosacea and acne vulgaris and the episodic and photo-aggravated nature of the eruptions, a diagnosis of actinic folliculitis was rendered. Phototesting was not performed owing to patient preference. Despite this, the clinical and histopathologic findings were considered sufficiently diagnostic. The patient initiated treatment with adapalene gel, 0.3%, and reported decreased severity of eruptions with fewer pustules and faster resolution. She was able to prevent recurrences with strict use of a solar umbrella in summer months. The treatment responses further supported the diagnosis. Actinic folliculitis is a monomorphic pustular dermatitis that presents on the face, with possible involvement of the arms and upper chest. The eruption normally occurs within 4 to 14 hours of sunlight exposure and resolves over 7 to 10 days.1,2This entity encompasses 2 previously separate disorders, acne aestivalis and actinic superficial folliculitis.1,3Acne aestivalis was previously described as a pruritic, papular eruption of the face induced by sunlight. Actinic superficial folliculitis is characterized by pustules distributed over the shoulders, upper trunk, and arms that typically appear 24 to 36 hours after sun exposure.1,3 Current case reports of actinic folliculitis in the literature describe patients between the ages of 17 and 42 years, but analysis regarding the average age at onset is lacking. The pathogenesis of the disease remains undetermined. However, some have hypothesized that epidermal thickening induced by UV radiation causes follicular infundibular occlusion, inflammation, and lesion development.2Histopathological descriptions in the literature include perifollicular mixed inflammatory infiltrate, perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and subcorneal pustulosis.1,3,4 The differential diagnosis of actinic folliculitis includes papulopustular rosacea, pinpoint papular light eruption, acute localized exanthematous pustulosis, acne vulgaris, and photoallergy. Papulopustular rosacea presents with papules and pustules overlying erythema in a central facial distribution. Biopsy results are often nonspecific and unnecessary for diagnosis, but characteristic histopathology includes mixed perivascular and perifollicular infiltrates in the superficial and mid-dermis with accumulation of neutrophils beyond the follicle.5Papulopustular rosacea was considered unlikely given the failed response to established rosacea treatment regimens. Pinpoint papular light eruption is a clinical variant of polymorphous light eruption characterized by pinpoint papules and vesicles 30 minutes to 3 days after UV light exposure, most commonly in dark-skinned individuals.6Histopathologic findings correspond to clinical course. Acute lesions are similar to those of classical polymorphous light eruption and show spongiosis, edema, and superficial and deep perivascular infiltrates. Subacute lesions consist of an atrophic epidermis with claw-like extension of epidermal rete around a well-circumscribed lichenoid infiltrate, mimicking lichen nitidus. Pustules are not a typical morphologic characteristic of pinpoint papular light eruption clinically or histologically, arguing against this diagnosis in this patient. Acute localized exanthematous pustulosis consists of acute-onset nonfollicular, sterile pustules on an erythematous background affecting the face, neck, and chest.7Most cases have been linked to drug hypersensitivity, but some reports describe associations with viral infection or insect bites.7These lesions are often accompanied by fever and neutrophilic leukocytosis. Histologically, acute localized exanthematous pustulosis presents as sterile subcorneal pustules with an edematous papillary dermis and mixed perivascular infiltrates. This patient’s history was negative for recent illness, systemic medications, or fever, rendering this diagnosis unlikely. Several treatment strategies have been proposed for actinic folliculitis. Adapalene, a topical retinoid, has been successful in preventing flares with application beginning a few weeks before sun exposure.2Other reports have described success with isotretinoin, including complete clearance and extended periods of remission.8Newer reports have explored the role of narrowband UV-B phototherapy, but more research is needed to determine its utility.9

C, Tissue biopsy results revealed multiple circumscribed nests of granulomas that were infiltrating the dermis and subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin). scenario: A school-aged boy experienced generalized erythematous rashes for 4 years. Skin examination showed ichthyosiform brownish plaques on his lower extremities and multiple erythematous confluent papules and plaques on his trunk and face (Figure, A and B). Topical steroid and pimecrolimus were administered, but their effects were limited. In addition, painful distal and proximal interphalangeal joints were noted for 2 years, and the patient could not clench his fists. Uveitis in both eyes was also diagnosed by an ophthalmologist. Microscopic examination of his hair showed no trichorrhexis invaginata or trichorrhexis nodosa. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained and submitted for further histopathologic analysis (Figure, C and D).
explanation: A skin biopsy from the ichthyosiform rash on the right arm showed small noncaseating granulomas, multinucleated giant cells, and neutrophil infiltration in the dermis and subcutis. Acid-fast staining, Gomori methenamine-silver staining, and modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining all showed an absence of microorganisms, and sarcoidosis was confirmed. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense variation (Arg334Trp) inNOD2that has previously been detected in Blau syndrome.1Accordingly, the diagnosis of Blau syndrome was confirmed. Blau syndrome is an autosomal dominant inflammatory disease characterized by a triad of granulomatous dermatitis, uveitis, and systemic polyarthritis. Variations inNOD2/CARD15on chromosome 16q12 have been identified in patients with Blau syndrome.NOD2/CARD15is primarily expressed in monocytes, a cell type capable of differentiation into multinucleated giant cells and epithelioid cells.2It has been hypothesized thatNOD2/CARD15variation is associated with increased NF-kB activation, macrophage death, and granulomatous inflammation.2 Skin involvement is one of the early manifestations of Blau syndrome. Early cutaneous presentations include morbilliform and lichenoid papules that mimic granuloma annulare, whereas the late manifestations are more diverse and include ichthyosiform rash, erythema nodosum-like nodules, and granulomatous vasculitis.3 Ocular involvement is one of the most disabling complications of Blau syndrome, causing loss of vision that may progress to blindness if left untreated. The common form of ocular involvement includes granulomatous panuveitis, cataracts, band keratopathy, iritis, and secondary glaucoma.4Arthritis usually appears during the first decade of life, with the wrist, metacarpophalangeal, metatarsophalangeal, and proximal interphalangeal joints being the joints most commonly involved.5Plain radiography often shows joint space narrowing and deformities with periarticular swelling, but without bone erosion. Patients with Blau syndrome rarely present with pulmonary involvement, and bilateral hilar adenopathy is often absent.6 Currently, to our knowledge, there is still no standard treatment for Blau syndrome, although corticosteroids are generally the first line of treatment. Additional immunomodulant agents or biologics (including methotrexate, tumor necrosis factor [TNF]–α inhibitor, and interleukin 1 receptor antagonist) may be added.1The patient in this article was treated with oral prednisolone in addition to methotrexate, but his skin eruptions and arthritis were only mildly responsive to those treatments. Because elevated serum TNF-α (17.9 pg/mL) levels were still noted, TNF-α inhibitor with adalimumab was administered, and the patient’s skin, arthritis, and uveitis all had satisfactory responses after adalimumab treatment for 6 months. Ichthyosiform rash is usually a late presentation of Blau syndrome.7The differential diagnoses of ichthyosiform rash include ichthyosis vulgaris, Netherton syndrome, and pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP). Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by variations inFLGand characterized by diffuse scaling of the skin since childhood, palmar hyperlinearity, and keratosis pilaris.8Ichthyosis vulgaris is associated with atopic dermatitis and typically manifests with early-onset chronic dry skin with severe pruritus. Histologically, ichthyosis vulgaris may present with a thin or absent granular cell layer. Netherton syndrome, which is caused by an autosomal recessive variation ofSPINK5, is often associated with atopic diathesis and other important clinical traits, such as ichthyosis, ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, and hair shaft abnormalities.9Histology shows psoriasiform rather than granulomatous dermatitis. However, ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis are not associated with uveitis or arthritis. Pityriasis rubra pilaris may be characterized as inherited ichthyosiform rashes.10Atypical juvenile-onset PRP (type V) was found to be associated withCARD14variations, which function as an activator of NF-kB signaling. Because the involved signaling pathway is similar, PRP and Blau syndrome also share similar manifestations, such as ichthyosiform scaling on the lower extremities and scaly patches involving the cheeks, with sparing of the infralabial region. The histopathology of PRP shows the presence of alternating parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis in vertical and horizontal directions. The present case highlights the characteristic manifestations of Blau syndrome. Early recognition of the disease aids in its early diagnosis and treatment and can help to prevent subsequent ocular and articular complications.1

Note the nail dystrophy in the left first toe. B, Detail of tense blisters and vesicles, erosions, and scar areas.
