scenario: A 24-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of sudden onset of headache, nausea, and binocular vertical diplopia. She denied any other neurologic symptoms. Her medical history included untreated hyperprolactinemia manifested by galactorrhea and oligomenorrhea. She did not take any medications, smoke, or drink alcohol. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect. There was minimal limitation in infraduction in the left eye with corresponding left hypertropia (Video), which was worse in left gaze and right head tilt. Ophthalmoscopy findings were normal in each eye. Visual field findings (Humphrey 24-2 algorithm) were normal in each eye as well.

options.A: Check thyrotropin and thyroid receptor autoantibody levels and order orbital imaging
options.B: Order acetylcholine receptor antibody level titers
options.C: Order urgent computed tomography scan and computed tomography angiography of the brain

answer: Order urgent computed tomography scan and computed tomography angiography of the brain
distractors: Check thyrotropin and thyroid receptor autoantibody levels and order orbital imaging
Order acetylcholine receptor antibody level titers
explanation: C. Order urgent computed tomography scan and computed tomography angiography of the brain The differential diagnosis for sudden onset of headache, nausea, and binocular vertical diplopia in a young patient is limited. The presence of left infraduction limitation and corresponding left hypertropia that does not fit the pattern for fourth nerve palsy could be because of partial third cranial nerve palsy. The relevant medical history of hyperprolactinemia makes pituitary apoplexy (ie, sudden hemorrhage within the pituitary gland, often within preexisting pituitary adenoma) and aneurysmal compression of the third nerve the most critical diagnoses to be ruled out. Thus, ordering an urgent computed tomography scan and computed tomography angiography scan of the brain with attention to the sellar region (choice C) would be the most appropriate course of action. Checking thyrotropin and thyroid autoantibody levels and ordering orbital imaging (choice A) would be correct if thyroid eye disease was the suspected culprit. However, sudden onset of headache and nausea is not a typical presentation of thyroid eye disease, making this diagnosis unlikely. While myasthenia gravis can present with vertical binocular diplopia, it would also not explain the sudden onset of headaches and nausea, and other likely signs of myasthenia gravis (eg, orbicularis oculi weakness and variable ptosis fatigable in sustained upgaze) were not present. Thus, ordering acetylcholine receptor antibody level titers (choice B) would not be the most important investigation. Lumbar puncture (choice D) would be the best test to order if subarachnoid hemorrhage were suspected as causing sudden onset of headache and nausea. However, computed tomography scan and computed tomography angiogram imaging are sensitive for identifying aneurysms and detecting blood in the subarachnoid space; thus it should be performed first. The clinical presentation of pituitary apoplexy is highly variable and largely determined by extent of hemorrhage, necrosis, and edema within the pituitary gland. Headache, typically with sudden and severe onset accompanied by nausea and vomiting, is a presenting symptom in more than 70% of patients and likely occurs because of dural traction and/or meningeal irritation secondary to extravasation of blood and necrotic material into subarachnoid space.1,2 Vision loss and visual field defects affect 70% of patients with pituitary apoplexy1due to sudden hemorrhage-related expansion of the pituitary grand and resultant compression of chiasm and prechiasmatic optic nerves. Oculomotor nerve palsies affect half of patients with pituitary apoplexy and occur because of sudden lateral expansion of pituitary tissue into cavernous sinuses, clearly visualized on the computed tomography scan of this patient.3The third nerve is the most frequently affected.3Altered consciousness or cerebral ischemia can occur in 15% of cases.4Frequently, there are no precipitating factors and up to 25% of patients are asymptomatic but hypertension, medications, surgery, coagulopathy, pregnancy and the postpartum period, head injury, radiation, or dynamic testing of the pituitary gland are potential risk factors.5 Endocrine dysfunction is an important source of morbidity in patients with pituitary apoplexy and can present before the apoplectic episode, causing menstrual disturbances, fatigue, or galactorrhea, as was the case here. Corticotropic deficiency is the most common3,6life-threatening hormonal complication, causing hemodynamic instability and hyponatremia and requiring corticosteroid supplementation.4 For patients with visual field defects and/or limited ocular motility, transsphenoidal hypophysectomy to decompress the visual pathway is preferred.1However, if pituitary function remains normal without chiasmal compression or ocular motility, observation can be appropriate.4 Computed tomography demonstrated a 1.0 × 1.2-cm high-density pituitary abnormality with evidence of blood within the pituitary gland (Figure), confirming the diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy. Pituitary hormone levels were normal, suggesting pituitary apoplexy may have caused infarction of the secretory adenoma, normalizing prolactin level. Therefore, conservative management was chosen.

scenario: A 65-year-old woman was referred with a 6-week history of blurry vision, ocular pain, and subconjunctival yellow discoloration in the left eye. Suspicious retinal detachment and intraocular mass were identified, which raised concerns for choroidal melanoma. No symptoms or signs were reported in the right eye. Her ocular history included bilateral cataract surgery 5 years prior. Review of systems yielded negative results, including for ocular trauma, jaundice, and cutaneous melanoma. She had no history of tobacco use. On examination of the left eye, visual acuity was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 8 mm Hg. The anterior segment showed diffuse conjunctival chemosis of yellow hue, low-grade aqueous reaction, and pseudophakia (Figure 1A). On the fundus evaluation, large pockets of subretinal fluid suggested choroidal effusion based on marked fluid shifting with head position. B-scan ultrasonography confirmed 4-quadrant choroidal hemorrhage and partially mobile serous retinal detachment. B-scans also exhibited a solid lesion from the 6- to 10-o’clock meridians with irregular shape and variable internal reflectivity, measuring 5.8 mm in height. Magnetic resonance imaging was requested to delineate the mass from the surrounding clot (Figure 1B). In the interim, she received oral steroids aiming to contain the abundant exudation and topical atropine for pain, evolving with minimal clinical improvement on these features.

options.B: Drain the hemorrhage with scleral windows
options.D: Rule out an occult systemic neoplasm

answer: Rule out an occult systemic neoplasm
distractors: Investigate liver dysfunction and biliary tract obstruction
Drain the hemorrhage with scleral windows
explanation: Choroidal metastasis from lung adenocarcinoma D. Rule out an occult systemic neoplasm Choroidal effusion consists of serous-hemorrhagic fluid accumulation in the suprachoroidal space typically encountered in trauma, surgery, or uveitis scenarios.1,2It can produce a mass effect simulating tumors2or be the presenting feature of ocular neoplasms,3requiring elucidation as to its origin and nature. In this patient, disproportional choroidal exudation in the context of a solid lesion unresponsive to steroid therapy was strongly suggestive of malignancy. The yellow discoloration noted in only 1 eye was unusual and likely reflected a subacute process related to long-standing choroidal fluid buildup.4Unlike the scleral impregnation with bilateral involvement classically seen in jaundice,5the ocular coloration changes developed in this patient indicated a local mechanism, mediated by fluid extravasation from the choroidal compartment to the subconjunctival space.4Therefore, screening for causes of bilirubin elevation, such as liver dysfunction and biliary tract obstruction (choice A), would not be the first step taken. Given the presence of an intraocular mass, primary and secondary neoplasms should be foremost investigated before any treatment consideration. Surgical drainage of the hemorrhagic content (choice B) and management with plaque brachytherapy (choice C) would not be advisable until a final diagnosis was reached because of risks of incomplete disease control and tumor seeding. Based on the characteristics of the lesion on imaging, notably heterogeneous reflectivity, irregular surface, and infiltrative pattern, which typically signal uveal metastasis as opposed to primary melanoma,6screening for an occult systemic primary cancer should be the first course of action (choice D). Accordingly, the patient underwent full-body imaging studies with computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis. She was identified with a 6 × 9-cm silent mass at the upper left pulmonary lobe with associated mediastinal adenopathy (Figure 2). A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the lung tumor revealed primary adenocarcinoma. Other metastatic lesions were also identified on the thoracic spine. Metastasis is the most common ocular malignancy in the adult population, affecting the choroid in 85% of patients by hematogenous dissemination.6,7Metastatic implants are visible on fundoscopy as single or multiple light-yellow solid lesions of variable shape usually with associated subretinal fluid.6Primary sites have been localized, in order of frequency, to breast, lung, kidney, gastrointestinal tract, and cutaneous melanoma.7In a large series, uveal metastasis from lung cancer was more prevalent in men (55%) and mainly unifocal (77%) and unilateral (82%).8Approximately 40% of individuals had the original tumor discovered only after detecting uveal lesions8similar to what we observed in this patient. Although choroidal effusion may be a nonspecific finding attributable to metastatic systemic neoplasms,3,6a threshold of suspicion for underlying malignancy is advisable in the face of any intraocular solid growth. The patient was treated with systemic chemotherapy (entrectinib) and external beam radiotherapy to the mediastinum and orbits (20 Gy, 5 fractions). The conjunctival color progressively recovered in the following weeks, whereas the choroidal metastasis and detachment resolved 3 months after radiation. The visual acuity in the left eye remained hand motion.

scenario: A 72-year-old woman presented with new-onset decreased vision in the right eye. Her ocular history included pseudoexfoliation syndrome and glaucomatous optic neuropathy in the right eye. Past ocular surgery included uncomplicated trabeculectomy in the right eye treated with mitomycin C (3 months prior) and no ocular surgery history in the left eye. Her medical history included pulmonaryMycobacterium aviuminfection secondary to hypogammaglobulinemia. Computed tomography scan 2 months prior exhibited reactivation and she started treatment with clarithromycin (1000 mg/d), ethambutol (15 mg/kg/d), and rifabutin (300 mg/d). Best-corrected visual acuity was hand motions OD and 20/20 OS. Intraocular pressures were 4 mm Hg ODand 13 mm Hg OS. Anterior segment examination of the right eye showed substantial conjunctival hyperemia and substantial cellular response in the anterior chamber (2 to 3+) along with a 1-mm hypopyon. There was no leak at the trabeculectomy bleb (negative Seidel test). B-scan ultrasonography showed no retinal detachment or mass. Presumed diagnosis of bleb-related infectious endophthalmitis was made and she was referred for treatment. Pars plana vitrectomy was performed, including vitreous sampling, and showed very light growth ofStaphylococcus aureusin 1 colony on 1 plate, which was highly suspicious for contaminant. Intravitreal amikacin and vancomycin were administered after vitreous sampling was performed. Postoperatively, the patient initiated treatment with topical antibiotics and corticosteroids. Her visual acuity returned to 20/30. Two months later, she presented again with a similar acute vision loss in the left eye (counting fingers). Anterior segment examination showed conjunctival hyperemia, cellular reaction, and a small hypopyon (Figure).

options.A: Pars plana vitrectomy with hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics
options.B: Treatment with topical and oral antibiotics
options.C: Review and adjust systemic medications and treat with topical corticosteroids
options.D: Treat with systemic and topical corticosteroids

answer: Review and adjust systemic medications and treat with topical corticosteroids
distractors: Pars plana vitrectomy with hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics
Treatment with topical and oral antibiotics
Treat with systemic and topical corticosteroids
explanation: C. Review and adjust systemic medications and treat with topical corticosteroids Pars plana vitrectomy with hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics would not be the preferred answer because with the lack of surgery history, an infections etiology would be lower on the differential diagnosis (choice A). Treatment with topical and oral antibiotics would not be the preferred answer because of the insufficient intraocular penetration (choice B). Treat with systemic and topical corticosteroids would not be the preferred answer because of the importance of investigating underlying etiology prior to treatment (choice D). Rifabutin is used for the treatment and prophylaxis of theM aviumcomplex (MAC) infection.1It is a semisynthetic derivative of rifamycin SV and has broad antimicrobial activity, including against MAC. It has been shown to have a dose-associated toxicity including polyarthralgia/arthritis, aphthous stomatitis, skin pigmentation, and uveitis.2Signs and symptoms of anterior uveitis with or without hypopyon, intermediate uveitis, and posterior uveitis or panuveitis may occur between 2 weeks and 7 months following the start of therapy. Symptoms can present with dosage as low as 300 mg/d.3,4Symptoms have been shown to worsen with increasing dose. Most cases resolve within 1 to 2 months of discontinuation of rifabutin and administration of topical corticosteroids. Published reports of rifabutin-associated uveitis have all been associated with concurrent medications like clarithromycin and fluconazole. These medications elevate serum rifabutin levels by inhibition of the hepatic microsomal cytochrome P-450 system that metabolizes rifabutin. This patient was taking concurrent clarithromycin as part of her MAC infection treatment.5,6Patients with rifabutin-associated uveitis have excellent visual prognosis, and most return to 20/30 visual acuity 3 weeks after initiating topical corticosteroid treatment, in some cases without requiring medication cessation.7 The initial clinical presentation of this patient was complicated by the recent history of trabeculectomy with mitomycin C. The constellation of conjunctival hyperemia, anterior chamber cellular reaction, hypopyon, and poor view of fundus in the context of trabeculectomy was highly suspicious for bleb-related infectious endophthalmitis. On clinical examination, the patient did not have a bleb leak or obvious blebitis. However, diagnosis of bleb-related endophthalmitis could not be excluded based on our clinical findings. Studies have shown that blebitis without bleb leak and blebitis with bleb leak present at a similar incidence (0.10% vs 0.11%).8Bleb-related endophthalmitis is one of the most serious sight-threatening late sequelae of trabeculectomy surgery for glaucoma. Treatment is extremely time sensitive. Therefore, in this clinical scenario, it was important for the patient to undergo immediate aqueous sampling to rule out infectious etiology and receive immediate hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics. The patient was referred back to her infectious disease specialist for discontinuation of rifabutin and consideration for alternative treatment of her MAC infection. Topical corticosteroid treatment was initiated, and the patient will be followed up closely.

scenario: An 80-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset bilateral horizontal diplopia accompanied by left-sided upper eyelid ptosis. explanation: Trigeminal schwannoma involving left cavernous sinus and the Meckel cave C. Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast This patient’s abnormalities comprise left sixth nerve palsy with ipsilateral Horner syndrome and trigeminal nerve palsy. This process localizes to the left cavernous sinus where the sixth nerve, trigeminal nerve, and sympathetic fibers travel in proximity: third-order sympathetic fibers from the hypothalamus exit the internal carotid artery adventitia and pass alongside the sixth nerve as it courses through the cavernous sinus. The trigeminal ganglion is located in the Meckel cave, a dura-lined cavity lateral to the cavernous sinus, where the peripheral trigeminal divisions originate. Divisions V1 and V2 are pure sensory nerves, whereas V3 also carries motor nerves involved in mastication, explaining impaired chewing and drooling in this patient. All 3 divisions enter the cavernous sinus after exiting the Meckel cave. While brainstem lesions can cause multiple cranial neuropathies, slow progression of symptoms without accompanying neurological deficits make this unlikely in this case. In this patient, high-resolution neuroimaging is the next best step (option C). CT angiography (option A) can reveal vascular abnormalities of the cavernous sinus but will not identify subtle nonvascular lesions. Here, long-standing trigeminal numbness suggests a compressive etiology best visualized on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Lumbar puncture (option B) can rule out infectious, neoplastic, or inflammatory processes but would not localize the pathology. Elevated inflammatory markers (option D) may suggest giant cell arteritis, which can rarely present with sixth nerve palsy. However, slow-evolving symptomatology in this patient and trigeminal nerve involvement essentially rule out this diagnosis. Brain MRI demonstrated an expansile lesion at the left cavernous sinus and the Meckel cave with extension into the pterygopalatine fossa and foramen ovale (Figure 2). Radiographic characteristics were consistent with trigeminal ganglion schwannoma with compression of adjacent structures. Subsequent cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal composition and cytology. Intracranial schwannomas are the most common benign intracranial tumor in adults following meningiomas and pituitary tumors.1Occurrence may be sporadic or in association with neurofibromatosis type 2, and malignant transformation is very rare.2,3Treatment entails surgical resection4,5or, increasingly, stereotactic radiosurgery.6Despite radiosurgery, approximately one-third of cases may progress and symptomatic improvement is seen in fewer than 50% owing to the challenging tumor location.7As in the present case, trigeminal schwannomas are often misdiagnosed as trigeminal neuralgia. Trigeminal neuralgia is a distinct syndrome characterized by short, recurrent episodes of sharp pain. Atypical cases may feature prolonged facial pain.8In contrast, trigeminal schwannomas frequently present with chronic facial parasthesias.9Diplopia is also common due to cavernous sinus involvement.5,9To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of trigeminal schwannoma presenting with abducens palsy and Horner syndrome. Ophthalmologists must assess for Horner syndrome in patients with new abducens nerve palsy, as this suggests cavernous sinus pathology and necessitates urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain. Recognizing atypical headache syndromes can help ophthalmologists identify cases requiring further investigation. The patient underwent radiotherapy in an attempt to reduce tumor burden. Unfortunately, the tumor size and accompanying symptoms remained unchanged.

caption: Imaging findings at presentation. A, Color fundus photograph of the right eye shows mild hyperemia and swelling of the optic disc along with moderate venous vessels tortuosity. B, Late-frame fluorescein angiography of the right eye shows mild dye leakage of the optic disc and no other obvious abnormalities.
scenario: A 14-year-old boy was referred to us because of ocular and periocular pain with photophobia in his right eye for the last 5 days. Aside from atopic dermatitis, his medical history was unremarkable. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Slitlamp examination of the right eye disclosed conjunctival hyperemia and ciliary congestion, anterior chamber flare 2+, and a few nongranulomatous keratic precipitates; the left anterior segment was quiet. Intraocular pressure was 15 mm Hg OU. Pupillary light responses were normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed 1+ of vitritis (binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy score) in the right eye and swelling of the optic disc in both eyes, to a greater extent in the right eye (Figure, A). Routine blood tests, including full blood cell count, plasma glucose levels, liver function test, and kidney function test, were performed on the same day and showed a serum creatinine level of 1.57 mg/dL (reference range: 0.5-1.0 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4). Antibodies anti–Treponema pallidumwere tested and the results were negative. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography at presentation showed increased thickness of the retinal nerve fiber layer in both eyes, to a greater extent in the right eye. Fluorescein angiography revealed dye leakage of the right optic disc (Figure, B); no further abnormalities were found in both eyes. Indocyanine green angiography findings were normal.

options.A: Start treatment with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics without further investigations
options.B: Order urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin test
options.C: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits

answer: Order urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin test
distractors: Start treatment with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics without further investigations
Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
explanation: Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome B. Order urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin test Starting topical treatment with corticosteroids and cycloplegic eye drops without further investigations (choice A) would not be the preferred answer because abnormal kidney function warrants further investigations. Indeed in this case, urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin (β2M) testing (choice B) revealed normoglycemic glycosuria and increased β2M levels (6.6 mg/24 h; reference range, 0.02-0.37), suggestive of tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome (TINU).1Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits (choice C) was not indicated as urgent investigation, because the observed optic disc edema was most likely secondary to the intraocular inflammation rather than a central nervous system dysfunction. However, MRI of the brain and orbits was performed electively and did not show any abnormalities. Finally, observation (choice D) in symptomatic and active uveitis is not recommended. TINU is a rare cause of uveitis accounting for less than 2% of cases of uveitis and mostly affecting young patients with a median age at onset of 15 years.2,3Prevalence of TINU may be underestimated because of lack of recognition mainly in patients without evidence of kidney dysfunction or when proper laboratory testing is not performed at the first presentation.4Diagnosis requires both tubulointerstitial nephritis, suggested by kidney dysfunction and urinalysis, and uveitis. Notably, both kidney and eye disease can be asymptomatic and have independent progression.2Kidney dysfunction, whose clinical presentation is usually nonspecific (rash, arthralgia, and fever), is the result of an acute kidney injury that can eventually lead to chronic kidney disease.2,5Urinalysis may be positive for proteinuria, glycosuria, and cells, while urinary β2M is increased in the vast majority of cases.4Kidney biopsy is the definitive diagnostic procedure to confirm tubulointerstitial nephritis. Hettinga et al,1though, have shown that increased urinary β2M, combined with increased serum creatinine levels, is a reliable marker with high positive and negative predictive values for the diagnosis and monitoring of TINU. Other causes of uveitis with possible kidney involvement, such as sarcoidosis, Behçet disease, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis, should always be excluded.1,2,6 Uveitis onset is variable but usually occurs 3 months after the onset of nephritis, and younger patients are more likely to develop a chronic course of uveitis (more than 3 months), despite proper treatment.2,7Although second-eye involvement can occur after presentation, uveitis is most commonly bilateral anterior.3Posterior ocular involvement or panuveitis are less common, although the optic disc may be involved in almost half of the patients at presentation.3-5,7,8Photophobia, loss of vision, and painful and red eye are the main presenting symptoms. The mainstay of treatment of TINU is topical and systemic corticosteroid therapy, which provides overall favorable outcomes. A close ophthalmic follow-up is recommended over the first year after the diagnosis, since recurrences are common and the use of immunomodulatory therapy is often needed.2,4 This patient presented with unilateral anterior uveitis and bilateral posterior ocular involvement, indicating that TINU may have a broad clinical presentation. Therefore TINU should be always considered as a possible cause of uveitis in pediatric population. A kidney biopsy to confirm the diagnosis was deemed unnecessary because of the morbidity of the procedure. The patient was given a tapering course of oral steroid and topical treatment of anterior uveitis. Both the uveitis and the kidney function dramatically improved after treatment. Optic disc edema improved 1 week after the start of oral steroid treatment and the patient was later switched to mycophenolate mofetil as a steroid-sparing agent. Mild disc swelling persisted over several months despite normal findings on repeated automated visual field examinations.

caption: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of macula demonstrating schisislike separation involving fovea (A) and OCT of optic nerve head, with optic pit marked with an arrowhead (B).
scenario: A 70-year-old woman with an ocular history of primary open-angle glaucoma on latanoprost, bilateral trabeculectomies, and argon laser trabeculoplasties presented with several months of worsening vision in the left eye. On examination, her best-corrected distance visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/60 OS (baseline 20/40 OU). Pupils were equally round and reactive, without afferent pupillary defect. Findings of Amsler grid testing were notable for a small area of distortion inferiorly in the left eye. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were 13 mm Hg in both eyes. Findings of anterior segment examination were unremarkable. Findings of dilated fundus examination were notable for cup-disc ratio of 0.9 in the right eye and 0.85 in the left eye with temporal thinning, stable from prior, and new intraretinal thickening in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging of the left eye revealed schiticlike separation of the outer plexiform and outer nuclear layers extending from the temporal edge of the optic nerve head to the fovea (Figure 1A), continuous with the peripapillary nerve sheath.

options.D: Genetic testing for the RS1 gene

distractors: Genetic testing for the RS1 gene
explanation: Macular retinoschisis in the setting of glaucomatous optic atrophy The patient’s decreased vision was due to macular retinoschisis, an abnormal splitting of the neuroretina associated with glaucomatous optic atrophy. Observation (choice C) is correct because the patient noted only mild distortion, and retinoschisis can remain stable1or resolve spontaneously2,3in up to 40% of cases.3Schisis can resolve after vitrectomy,1so surgery (choice A) could be pursued if symptoms worsened. Barrier laser (choice B), as described by Prinzi et al,4has been used to treat retinoschisis in glaucoma; however, peripapillary laser photocoagulation carries risk of vision loss and the patient had only a 2-line decrease in vision. Testing for theRS1gene (choice D) would be indicated if X-linked retinoschisis was suspected; however, this disease appears almost exclusively in boys. Retinoschisis is rare in patients with glaucoma, with a reported rate of 5.9%3in 1 study. In this study, retinoschisis in glaucoma originated from the optic disc and overlapped with retinal nerve fiber layer defects, suggesting that schisis correlates with glaucomatous damage to the optic nerve head. Similarly, patients with schisis had worse visual field mean deviations compared with patients without.3Approximately one-third of eyes with schisis also had an acquired optic disc pit (aODP).3The relationship between glaucoma, aODPs, and retinoschisis is unclear. aODPs may represent areas of increased susceptibility owing to damage from glaucoma5and could be an entry point for liquified vitreous to enter the retina, initiating retinoschisis.6Therefore, the presence of an aODP in a patient with glaucoma could increase the likelihood of retinoschisis development. The patient had an optic disc pit that was visible on OCT imaging at the time of schisis onset (Figure 1B). The contribution of IOP to retinoschisis in glaucoma is not well understood. In 1 study, patients with glaucoma with retinoschisis at the initiation of the study had higher IOPs than patients without retinoschisis.3However, retinoschisis has also been reported in normal tension glaucoma,7suggesting high IOP is not a requisite for retinoschisis development. Patients who developed retinoschisis over time did not have changes in IOP before and after retinoschisis development, suggesting IOP fluctuations are not causative.3Interestingly, resolution of retinoschisis was associated with either trabeculectomy or the initiation of IOP-lowering medications. Similarly, there are case reports of retinoschisis resolving after glaucoma surgery.1,8In this patient, IOP had been well controlled prior to schisis development and no trigger could be identified, suggesting that it was the result of chronic glaucomatous damage rather than an acute process. In conclusion, the development of macular retinoschisis is associated with glaucoma and can cause decreased visual acuity in a patient with glaucoma, even with well-controlled IOP. Mild vision loss can be managed conservatively with observation. The patient was monitored with serial OCT imaging, which showed gradual improvement of the schisis over an 18-month period (Figure 2), with residual persistence along the nasal edge of the macula and return of visual acuity to baseline of 20/40 OU. The patient’s glaucoma continued to be successfully managed medically.

caption: A, Fundus photograph shows scattered, punctate hypopigmentation and subtle irregular hyperpigmentation in the macula. B, Fundus autofluorescence shows irregularly distributed, speckled hypoautofluorescence, most prominent in the inferior macula. Findings were similar, although not symmetric in distribution, in the left eye.
scenario: A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed irregularly distributed speckled hypoautofluorescence in the posterior pole of each eye (Figure).

options.A: Inform patient that she has changes from drug toxicity
options.B: Initiate nutritional supplement therapy for treatment of age-related macular degeneration per Age-Related Eye Disease Study recommendations
options.C: Advise patient that family members are at risk for pattern dystrophy
options.D: Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid

answer: Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid
distractors: Inform patient that she has changes from drug toxicity
Initiate nutritional supplement therapy for treatment of age-related macular degeneration per Age-Related Eye Disease Study recommendations
Advise patient that family members are at risk for pattern dystrophy
explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

caption: Temporal artery biopsy specimen, histopathologic examination findings. A, Examination showed nonspecific lymphocytic infiltrate in the adventitia (arrowheads) and pale, amorphous, eosinophilic amyloid deposits (asterisk) in the muscularis of the vessel wall (original magnification ×25). B, Congo red staining with polarization microscopy results highlight characteristic apple-green birefringent deposits (arrowhead) (original magnification ×25).
scenario: A patient in their late 70s with a history of Crohn disease, coronary artery disease, hypercholesterolemia, and transient ischemic attack presented with sudden, painless, left-sided vision loss. They denied headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw claudication. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 103 mm/h and a magnetic resonance angiographic examination of the brain was negative for mass, infarction, and hemorrhage. Examination results of a right, superficial, temporal artery biopsy specimen showed chronic, nongranulomatous inflammation surrounding adventitial vessels and extensive subintimal fibrosis, without giant cells or segmental loss of the internal elastic lamina, which was interpreted as compatible with temporal arteritis. High-dose corticosteroid therapy was initiated (1 g methylprednisolone intravenously for 3 days followed by 60 mg/d of oral prednisone). A neuro-ophthalmologic examination performed 1 week later showed an unreactive left pupil with an obvious relative afferent pupillary defect. Optic nerve pallor concomitant with edema and a single flame-shaped hemorrhage at the 4-o’clock position on the disc margin was also observed. Two weeks later, persistent elevation of the ESR and C-reactive protein levels, despite continued oral prednisone therapy, prompted a review of the temporal artery biopsy findings. This disclosed abundant transmural deposits of amorphous eosinophilic acellular material that was congophilic and exhibited apple-green birefringence under polarized light, consistent with amyloid deposits (Figure). Immunohistochemical staining showed IgM and λ light chain restriction.

options.C: Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis
options.D: Order a biopsy of the liver

answer: Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis
distractors: Order a biopsy of the liver
explanation: Systemic amyloidosis in the setting of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia) C. Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis An older patient presenting with visual loss and pallid disc edema arouses suspicion for an anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. As the most common vasculitis of older adults in North America, giant cell arteritis (GCA) has become the poster child of the arteritic form of anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Well established as visually morbid—with an approximate 8% rate of permanent vision loss and a 50% rate of fellow eye involvement—and responsive to corticosteroid therapy, GCA has a low threshold for diagnosis and treatment.1However, the prevailing criteria for diagnosing GCA (the 1990 American College of Rheumatology classification) is relatively nonspecific, having a specificity of 91.3%.2Other vasculitides, including eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, hypersensitivity vasculitis, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, polyarteritis nodosa, and Takayasu arteritis, are all cited as misclassifications for GCA in the original article by Hunder et al.2 Classic histopathologic findings of GCA include marked narrowing of the arterial lumen by concentric intimal fibroplasia and transmural infiltrate of lymphocytes and macrophages (with or without giant cells), leading to fragmentation, multilamination, and segmental loss of the internal elastic lamina. In chronic cases, a fibrous or fibrovascular scar is present at the level of the internal elastic lamina and frequently involves the tunica media. Examination results of the patient’s temporal artery biopsy specimen were notable for chronic lymphocytic inflammation confined to the adventitia without an appreciable granulomatous component in the vessel wall or breaks in the internal elastic lamina. Although these findings are nondiagnostic for temporal arteritis, they should prompt additional tissue sampling to definitively exclude GCA and call to mind alternative etiologies of adventitial inflammation.3,4Intravitreal corticosteroid therapies have not been shown to significantly improve visual acuity in patients with ischemic optic neuropathy (choice A).5 Patients with clinically diagnosed GCA and partial or absent symptomatic response to corticosteroid therapies should be considered for alternative diagnoses. This includes amyloid deposition in the vessel wall, which may contribute to vision loss via vascular occlusion induced by the amyloid deposit itself or in combination with an inflammatory infiltrate. In the patient, temporal artery amyloidosis was discovered after 1 month of stable vision with persistently elevated inflammatory markers, emblematic of the diagnostic delay frequently seen in these cases. Factors contributing to delay include histopathologic examination misdiagnosis of amyloid as “intimal thickening” or “fibromyxoid change,” and partial clinical improvement with corticosteroid therapy.6Failure to recognize systemic disease has potentially grave implications, as amyloid light chain amyloidosis has an estimated 30% mortality rate within 18 months.7 Patients with temporal artery amyloidosis have a plasma cell dyscrasia in approximately 80% of cases, often in the setting of plasma cell myeloma, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and, less frequently, mature B-cell lymphomas.6Thus, systemic workup for underlying hematolymphoid dyscrasia is warranted and GCA-indicated medications, such as tocilizumab (choice B), are inappropriate. The standard laboratory evaluation includes complete blood cell count with differential and serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (choice C) for monoclonal immunoglobulin. In addition, a positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan, bone survey, and bone marrow biopsy are performed for comprehensive oncologic examination. According to consensus guidelines, performing a liver biopsy is not indicated (choice D) unless end-organ dysfunction is suspected.8 Approximately 1 week after the diagnosis of temporal artery amyloidosis, the patient developed a left footdrop and was hospitalized for uncontrolled atrial fibrillation. Results of a stroke workup were negative for evidence of cerebrovascular accident. Laboratory studies were notable for an elevated ESR of 130 mm/h and mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 10.2 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10). Serum protein electrophoresis testing with immunofixation showed marked elevation of IgM (5214 mg/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 0.01]) and free κ light chains (1200 mg/L; reference, 3.3-19.4 mg/L). Examination of the bone marrow biopsy specimen showed a 60% involvement by lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, confirming the diagnosis of IgM-associated monoclonal gammopathy, or Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Treatment with rituximab and bortezomib therapy was initiated.

caption: A, Low-powered hematoxylin-eosin stain of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma and numerous ectatic vascular channels (original magnification ×200). B, Coronal postcontrast T1 fat-saturated image acquired in a 3-T magnet.
scenario: A 16-year-old male with a history of mild seasonal allergies presented with right-sided congestion, thick discolored nasal drainage, facial pain/pressure, anosmia, and intermittent epistaxis for approximately 1 year. Nasal endoscopy revealed moderate global deviation of the septum to the left. On the right, thick mucus and crusting anterior to the middle turbinate was seen, completely occluding the nasal cavity. Physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous, expansile mass measuring 6 (anteroposterior) × 3.1 (transverse) × 5 (craniocaudal) cm within the right nasal cavity extending to the nasopharynx, with obliteration of the nasopharyngeal airway and anteroinferior displacement of the soft palate (Figure, B). The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. It crossed the midline to fill the nasopharynx and extended inferiorly toward the oropharynx. The mass was noted to originate at the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. Pathologic evaluation showed fragments of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma, numerous ectatic vascular channels, and a sprinkling of inflammatory cells (Figure, A). The surface epithelium was largely ulcerated, covered with fibrinous and inflammatory debris and bacterial colonies. Immunostaining showed CD31 and CD34 positivity. Stromal cells did not have β-catenin present. Elastic stain results showed scant elastic fibers in the vascular proliferation.
explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

caption: Computed tomography (CT) images of 2 brothers with bilateral lesions in the olfactory clefts. A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. B, Reformatted conventional CT scan in the 76-year-old brother showed similar findings.
scenario: Two brothers, aged 69 and 76 years, were independently referred to our center in the same week for evaluation of a right olfactory cleft tumor that had been progressively developing over several years. The brothers had not been in contact with each other for many years. Neither had a history of chronic rhinosinusitis. The 69-year-old patient had a medical history of benign prostatic hypertrophy and prior septoplasty. The 76-year-old brother had no relevant medical or surgical history. Both brothers reported an ipsilateral nasal obstruction, with no other significant symptoms. Clinical examination on both patients revealed a lesion originating from the right olfactory cleft. Imaging studies were performed to further characterize the findings. A computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral masses causing widening of the olfactory clefts, with the right-sided lesion being larger than the left and causing nasal bone thinning in both patients (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a smooth, larger, right-sided lesion in the olfactory clefts with heterogeneous T2 signal and heterogenous contrast enhancement, along with a smaller lesion on the left side.
explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

caption: A, Transaxial positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) image showing intense bilateral symmetric tonsillar hypermetabolism and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy hypermetabolism. B, Low-powered (original magnification ×40) and high-powered (inset; original magnification ×400) hematoxylin-eosin stain after tonsillectomy showing lymphoid follicular hyperplasia with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate.
scenario: A previously healthy 67-year-old man was referred to the otolaryngology department due to a progressively worsening sore throat over several weeks that was associated with an unintentional 5-kg weight loss and night sweats. The patient did not report recent travel, nor autoimmune conditions, and reported only heterosexual intercourse. A physical examination revealed a mobile, nontender left-sided jugular lymph node. Dentition and oropharyngeal examinations were unremarkable. Results of flexible laryngoscopy were normal. Routine blood work findings showed an elevated C-reactive protein level and a polyclonal elevation of gamma globulins. Complete blood cell count, kidney markers, and liver enzymes were normal. Computed tomographic (CT) angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable. Due to substantial worsening of the patient’s symptoms during the next weeks, positron emission tomography/CT was performed, with results showing intense bilateral tonsillar hypermetabolism and abnormal lymph node hypermetabolism above and below the diaphragm (Figure 1A). The patient underwent unilateral tonsillectomy followed by a course of antibiotics and prednisone. On pathologic examination, the tonsils showed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia associated with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate without abnormal lymphoid cells and plasmocytes (Figure 1B). Further exploration of the patient’s history revealed that 1 year before the otolaryngology evaluation, he developed a cutaneous eruption on the trunk.

options.B: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the tonsil

distractors: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the tonsil
explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

caption: A, Magnetic resonance imaging (T2-weighted) shows a hypervascular tumor over left nasal cavity with obstructive rhinosinusitis at frontal and ethmoid sinuses. B, Gross examination reveals a 4.8 × 3.0 × 1.8-cm whitish to pink-tan tumor.
scenario: A 65-year-old man presented to an outpatient department with a 2-year history of left nasal obstruction. He had a history of hypertension and was taking oral medication (amlodipine [5 mg]/valsartan [80 mg] and indapamide [1.5 mg] once daily) but had poorly controlled systolic blood pressure ranging from 130 to 160 mm Hg. No associated trauma or surgical history was reported. Physical examination revealed a large tumor originating from the olfactory groove in the left nasal cavity, with feeding vessels pushing the middle turbinate outward. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined and strongly enhancing mass in the left nasal cavity, with obstructive rhinosinusitis in the frontal and ethmoid sinuses (Figure 1A). During surgical exploration, the tumor abutted the superior end of the nasal septum near the cribriform plate. Tumor excision was completed with a surgical margin of at least 5 mm, with the perichondrium of the nasal septum as the deep margin. The feeding vessels of the tumors were cauterized during the resection. Gross examination revealed a 4.8 × 3.0 × 1.8-cm whitish to pink-tan mass lesion (Figure 1B). Histopathological examination revealed sheetlike proliferation of monomorphic ovoid to spindle tumor cells containing ectatic vascular spaces. In addition, immunohistochemical staining showed positive staining for smooth-muscle actin, cyclin D1, and nuclear expression of β-catenin and negative staining for epithelial membrane antigen, cytokeratin, and CD34.
explanation: Sinonasal glomangiopericytoma (GPC) is a relatively rare mesenchymal neoplasm located in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses.1,2It was first described by Stout and Murray in 1924 and was initially categorized as a hemangiopericytomalike neoplasm with perivascular myoid differentiation with a relatively benign clinical course.3,4It was described as an indolent tumor with low malignancy potential and accounts for less than 0.5% of all sinonasal tumors.5,6There is a slight female predominance reported and it commonly occurs in patients in the sixth and seventh decades of age.2,4The common clinical manifestations include nasal obstruction and epistaxis.2,6GPC is usually large in size when diagnosed due to its indolent characteristic and nonspecific presentations. Grossly, GPC is submucosal in nature with a smooth surface and polypoid appearance and is sometimes difficult to differentiate from inflammatory polyps under endoscopy, leading to a challenging early diagnosis.4However, inflammatory nasal polyps usually present as bilateral nasal disease and seldom contain feeding vessels. For this patient, diagnosis was made through pathologic examination, which revealed a diffuse, subepithelial proliferation of bland, uniform, closely packed spindled cells surrounding capillaries with perivascular hyalinization (Figure 2); thus, it was previously categorized as a hemangiopericytoma.7A positive immunohistochemical stain for smooth-muscle actin, cyclin D1, and nuclear expression of β-catenin can confirm the diagnosis of GPC. Grossly, both GPC and lobular capillary hemangiomas are polypoid submucosal lesions with smooth surfaces.7However, it is still difficult to distinguish between these lesions because they usually present with a solid and soft texture. Histologically, lobular capillary hemangioma reveals lobular vascular proliferation consisting of vessels of capillary caliber.8On the other hand, inverted papilloma is mucosal origin with cerebriform, lobulated, and firm appearance.6,9In contrast to GPC, inverted papilloma shows male predominance with a 2 to 3:1 male:female ratio and usually arises from maxillary sinus and lateral nasal wall.9In histology, inverted papilloma exhibits squamous epithelial cells within the sinonasal tract, a distinguishing histological feature that sets it apart from GPC.10Solitary fibrous tumors resemble GPC under microscopic histology, but in contrast to GPC, solitary fibrous tumors are immunoreactive for CD34. The etiology of GPC is still unknown, but hypervascularity caused by hypertension, trauma, pregnancy, and the use of corticosteroids have been reported as possible causes.6,7We presumed that long-term hypertension without adequate control might be the possible etiology in this patient. Complete surgical resection with adequate margins remains the primary management strategy in patients with GPC. Recurrences were infrequently documented, with the majority of such instances attributed to incomplete resection; notably, these recurrences manifested predominantly within 1 year after surgery.4Further, owing to the bleeding tendency, preoperative angiographic embolization of GPC feeding vessels has been suggested to reduce bleeding volume during surgical resection.1,4Radiotherapy was reported to be used in conjunction with surgery for local control of the disease.4Chemotherapy was additionally administered to patients presenting with metastatic disease, wherein the metastatic incidence was documented to range from 5% to 10%. It is noteworthy that this observation predates the formal classification of GPC as a distinct clinical entity in 2005, thus potentially introducing a risk of diagnostic misclassification.6Because of its rarity, no formal guidelines have been published for sinonasal GPC, to our knowledge. Sinonasal GPC is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm of the sinonasal tract. It is typically indolent and has low malignant potential, with nasal obstruction and epistaxis being the most common clinical manifestations. The diagnosis is made through histology and immunohistochemical staining, and complete surgical resection with adequate margins remains the standard management. The patient was regularly followed up at our outpatient department after surgery, and there was no tumor recurrence or decreased olfaction during the 3-year follow-up period.

caption: A, Axial cut of computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck demonstrating free air in the left lobe of the thyroid gland (arrowheads). B, Sagittal cut of neck CT scan showing 2-cm radiodense osseous foreign body in the upper cervical esophagus at C6 level (arrowhead). C, Coronal cut of CT scan showing gas in the thyroid gland (arrowheads).
scenario: A healthy patient in their teens presented to the emergency department with high-grade fever (38.7 °C), neck pain, and a foreign body sensation in the throat after eating chicken 3 days prior. Laboratory investigations demonstrated an elevated leukocyte count (22 500/µL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Lateral soft tissue radiography showed a radio-opaque foreign body at the level of C6. Computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed a 2-cm radio-opaque osseous foreign body at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle with signs of esophageal perforation, including air leak tracking toward the left lobe of the thyroid gland (Figure, A and B). The patient was brought to the operating room, and the esophageal foreign body was successfully removed. Postoperatively, the patient continued to become febrile despite intravenous antibiotic therapy. A repeated CT scan of the neck and chest was done (Figure, C).
explanation: This case is a great example of the clinical implications of cervical anatomy. The fascial layers of the neck are complex and can be divided into the superficial and deep layers. The deep cervical fascia can be further classified into the superficial (investing), middle, and deep layers. The middle layer is subdivided into the muscular and visceral layers, with the latter surrounding the anterior viscera of the neck, including the thyroid gland, trachea, and esophagus.1Given that both the esophagus and thyroid gland are enveloped in the visceral portion of the middle layer of the deep cervical fascia, one can anticipate how an esophageal perforation can result in air infiltrating the thyroid parenchyma. The resulting inflammation then leads to the clinical picture of emphysematous thyroiditis (ET).1,2 Signs and symptoms of ET that have been described in the literature include severe neck pain, dysphagia, dysphonia, and stridor.1Additionally, patients may have a toxic appearance and exhibit signs of tachycardia, high-grade fever, and rigors.2,3Physical examination may reveal neck swelling and cellulitis.2,3Crepitus may not be appreciated due to the deep location of the thyroid gland within the fascial layers of the neck.3 Imaging studies of the neck showing gas in the thyroid region are pathognomonic for acute ET.2Laboratory test results may show a significantly elevated white blood cell count along with other inflammatory markers.3In addition, results of thyroid function tests and thyroid antibody testing may be initially normal; however, the patient reported by Gigot et al3developed hypothyroidism 4 months later. This may be explained by the pyogenic destruction of thyroid tissue.3On the other hand, the current patient exhibited laboratory results indicating hyperthyroidism; however, the patient did not experience any signs or symptoms of hyperthyroidism. The most common cause among cases reviewed in the literature was infection withClostridium perfringens.3In addition, multinodular goiter was found in 4 of the 6 patients reported by Gigot et al,3which places these patients at higher risk of developing an anaerobic infection due to the increased incidence of areas with anoxic thyroid tissue. Penetrating injury to the neck was another cause that led to ET reported in the literature, although the injury was not associated with injury to the esophagus or trachea.2 Treatment of ET is aimed at treating the cause and may be either medical or surgical.2,3The majority of patients (5 out of 6) who were reviewed by Gigot et al3underwent incision and drainage, and 4 also received antibiotics. One patient received medical therapy to treat ET and needed large doses of intramuscular penicillin.3Meanwhile, the patient reported by Karadağ et al,2who developed ET after a penetrating neck trauma, was treated conservatively without any surgical intervention and made an unremarkable recovery after close follow-up. The current patient remained afebrile after the fourth postoperative day and made an unremarkable recovery for the remainder of the hospital stay. Esophageal perforation showed evidence of closure on postoperative day 9. The patient was therefore deemed fit for discharge and was sent home and prescribed oral amoxicillin-clavulanate treatment for 7 days. A follow-up appointment with otolaryngology 3 weeks after discharge revealed that the patient was doing well, with no evidence of dysphagia, neck pain, or fever, and had an unremarkable physical examination. Results of repeated thyroid function tests during the patient’s follow-up with endocrinology 6 weeks after discharge showed almost complete normalization.

caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
scenario: A 64-year-old man with a 2-year history of seizure disorder presented to the emergency department (ED) at an outside hospital with breakthrough seizures. One month prior to his ED visit, he had been treated with oral antibiotics when he presented to an urgent care center with left-sided otorrhea, otalgia, and hearing loss. In the ED, he denied headaches, fever, otalgia, otorrhea, or hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast showed diffuse enhancement and possible coalescence in the left mastoid process with adjacent dural enhancement and sigmoid sinus occlusion. He received intravenous vancomycin and cefepime and was started on a heparin drip before being transferred to our facility. On presentation at our facility, the patient appeared well with normal vital signs. There was no periauricular swelling or erythema. Otoscopic examination showed no inflammation of the external auditory canals, and the tympanic membranes were translucent without evidence of retraction or effusion. Computed tomographic venogram confirmed occlusion of the left transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and computed tomography of the temporal bone showed coalescence of mastoid air cells with erosion into the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was performed for biopsy and culture specimens. Histologic findings from the specimens demonstrated cells with oval nuclei and abundant cytoplasm arranged in syncytial clusters with occasional whorls, pseudoinclusions, and psammomatous calcifications (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical stains were positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and vimentin (Figure, B).

options.C: Acute coalescent mastoiditis with sigmoid sinus thrombosis

distractors: Acute coalescent mastoiditis with sigmoid sinus thrombosis
explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults.
